t: #3825 Longest Strictly Increasing Subsequence With Non-Zero Bitwise AND
o: A bitwise AND of several numbers is non-zero exactly when at least one bit position is set in every chosen number. So any valid subsequence is entirely contained in the set of numbers sharing some common bit b. That decomposes the problem: for each of the ≤30 bit positions, run a standard strictly-increasing LIS restricted to numbers having that bit, and take the maximum length. In [2,3,6]: bit 1 is shared by 2,3,6 whose LIS is 3 → answer 3. In [5,4,7]: bit 0 shared by 5,7 gives LIS 2. In [0,1], bit 0 shared by 1 gives 1. With n = 1e5 and 30 bits, 30 independent O(n log n) LIS runs fit comfortably.
k: AND > 0 ⇔ some single bit is common to all elements — enumerate the bit.
Per-bit LIS with patience sorting (binary search on tails) costs O(n log n).
All-zero arrays yield 0 because no bit is ever set.

a.i: For each bit b, keep a tails array where tails[t] is the smallest possible tail of a strictly increasing subsequence of length t+1 using only numbers with bit b set. Binary search gives the insertion point; extending or replacing keeps tails sorted, so each element costs O(log n).
s: Let B be the bit length of the maximum value.
For each bit b in [0, B): reset tails to empty.
Scan nums; for each x with bit b set, binary-search tails for x and insert/replace.
Answer is the maximum tails size across all bits (0 if no bit ever applies).
a.t: O(30 · n log n) — thirty LIS passes, each with a binary search per element.
a.sp: O(n) — the tails array per bit.

a.n: Approach 2: Single Pass with 30 Tail Arrays
a.i: Instead of rescanning nums for each bit, maintain all 30 tails arrays at once and update only those bits present in the current element. Same asymptotics but one traversal of the data, which helps when the array lives in slow memory.
s: Create an array of 30 empty tails lists.
For each x, for each set bit b of x, do the patience update on tails[b].
Track running maximum of tails lengths; return it.
a.t: O(30 · n log n) — each element triggers up to 30 logarithmic updates.
a.sp: O(30 · n) — all tails arrays coexist.

w: Both approaches are equivalent in cost; Approach 1 is easier to explain, Approach 2 has better cache behavior. Common mistakes: using bisect_right (breaks strictness for duplicates), forgetting that a lone element with a set bit counts as length 1, and missing the all-zeros → 0 edge case. Follow-ups: what if values were 64-bit (just raise the bit bound), or if you needed the actual subsequence (store parent pointers per bit).
